Description

Dorsal horn neurons are held in check by GABA acting on GABA-A receptors and glycine acting on glycine receptors, channels that let chloride in. The chloride gradient that makes these currents inhibitory is kept by the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2, which moves chloride out. BDNF acting through TrkB lowers KCC2, so the same transmitters inhibit less. PGE2 acting through EP2 and PKA phosphorylates the α3 subunit of the glycine receptor and reduces glycinergic inhibition in inflammatory pain. Many patients with painful knee OA show signs of central sensitisation, such as enhanced temporal summation.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Metabolites take a lighter shade of the same colour. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

KCC2, GABA, glycine and their receptors are blue: they hold dorsal horn neurons in check. The block shows their loss, which raises pain: BDNF and TrkB (red) lower KCC2, and PKA phosphorylates the glycine receptor α3 subunit and reduces glycinergic inhibition. The phosphorylated receptor keeps its blue, as it is the same molecule, though it inhibits less.
